consensus_summary: The lion chiefly signifies royal power, strength, and victory, preeminently Christ as the Lion of Judah, while remaining polyvalent enough to represent Satan, divine judgment, hostile rulers and empires, courage, and other contextual meanings.
book_summary: The lion signifies royal and predatory rulership or imperial power. Wicked rulers, Assyria, Babylon, and Israelite princes misuse this devouring power, while Christ is its rightful bearer as the Lion of Judah.
consensus_core_identification: Royal or sovereign power, chiefly identified with the messianic Christ, with context-dependent hostile and predatory applications.
book_core_identification: Royal, devouring rulership or empire, negatively instantiated by wicked rulers and kingdoms and rightfully embodied by the Lion of Judah.
boundary_disagreement: The book consolidates Christ, wicked rulers, and hostile empires under one ruler-or-empire category and makes devouring rulership central. It excludes or leaves outside the definition several consensus-recognized uses, especially Satan, generic courage, divine judgment apart from rulership, peaceful creation imagery, and evangelistic iconography.
material_contradiction: There is no direct contradiction: both identify Christ as the Lion of Judah and recognize rulers and empires as lion referents. The disagreement concerns the symbol’s organizing category and range, not replacement of the central referent.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus association with royal power and Christ while elevating a listed consensus alternative—predatory rulers and empires—into the governing definition. This materially narrows and reclassifies the lion’s accepted applications without denying the Christological identification, so REFINED is more appropriate than MATCH, DIVERGENT, or NOVEL.
strongest_objection: The printed texts strongly support lions as wicked rulers, princes, Assyria, Babylon, and Christ, but they do not establish that every significant biblical lion use belongs to the ruler-or-empire category; the book’s synthesis may therefore be overly restrictive.
